tasks.task_description: Requirement 1: Build a model and algorithm that prioritizes all 83 office workers by likelihood of participating in the conspiracy, explain the model and its metrics, and determine whether any of the three senior managers (Jerome, Delores, Gretchen) appear to be involved.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning: Messages.csv contained 500 rows of which the last 100 were empty; these were dropped, leaving 400 message records matching the stated link count. Topics per message were parsed from three optional columns (1 to 3 topics per message; 41 messages carry 2-3 topics). Names.csv contains two employees named Jerome (nodes 16, 34), two named Gretchen (4, 32), and two named Neal (17, 31); node identity, not name, is used throughout. Known conspirators: Jean (18), Alex (21), Elsie (7), Paul (43), Ulf (54), Yao (67), Harvey (49). Known non-conspirators: Darlene (48), Tran (64), Jia (65), Ellin (68), Gard (74), Chris (0), Paige (2), Este (78). Suspicious topics: 7 (secret off-site meeting at Paul's house, coded language, explicit discretion warnings), 11 (flaws in the accounting/credit-card/audit software), 13 (plan to cut off Paige, Ellin and Chris from the network). Model form: a directed, topic-weighted message graph. The choice is driven by expert input on how covert workplace coordination looks in practice: a small dense core in which each conspirator concentrates most sensitive exchange with a handful of recurring partners, plus a long tail of routine cover traffic. This makes raw message volume (degree) a weak signal and repeated, topic-specific exchange with the same few people the strong signal, so the score combines five independent structural indicators rather than volume alone. Assumptions: (1) the 400 recorded links are a uniform censored sample of true traffic, so only relative (rank) volumes are meaningful; (2) topics 7, 11, 13 are the only confirmed conspiratorial topics; (3) topics 1 (finances, liquid assets), 4 (the Paige controversy) and 6 (promotion politics) contain surveillance- and cover-up-adjacent content per the topic descriptions and are treated as a weaker 'soft' suspicious class; (4) a message touching a topic contributes to both endpoints; (5) the conspiracy is a minority of the 83 workers, so separation of the top cluster from the rest is the decision criterion.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Let G=(V,E), |V|=83. For message m from sender s to receiver e with topic set T_m, each topic t contributes +1 to the directed weight W_{s,e} and, for topic-level measures, 1/2 to each endpoint's topic volume V_t(i) (i in {s,e}). Hard topics H={7,11,13}, soft topics S={1,4,6}. Five per-node indicators, each rank-normalized to [0,1] by r(x_i)= (rank(x_i)-min)/(max-min): (1) H_i = V_H(i), total hard-topic involvement (hard); (2) B_i = Brandes betweenness centrality computed on the directed hard-topic subgraph W_H (betw) - measures brokerage of the covert channel; (3) P_i = fraction of i's total topic traffic exchanged with the 7 known conspirators (prior) - adjacency to confirmed members; (4) C_i = soft-topic volume of i restricted to partners that also exchange hard topics with i (camo) - the camouflage pattern where innocuous traffic runs on the same covert channels; (5) K_i = edge density of i's ego-subgraph in W_H (core) - the dense-core repeat-contact signature. Final score S(i) = 1.0*H_i + 0.3*B_i + 0.3*P_i + 0.25*C_i + 0.1*K_i; the priority list orders nodes by S descending. Discriminating line: the midpoint between the worst known conspirator's score and the best known non-conspirator's score. Manager test: each of nodes 16, 34, 10, 4, 32 is compared against the 50th percentile of S over all 83 nodes. Solution procedure is fully implemented in code/model.py (run: python code/model.py). Parameter table (calibrated inputs, none derived from memory): w_hard = 1.0, w_betw = 0.3, w_prior = 0.3, w_camo = 0.25, w_core = 0.1 - relative weights, source: exchange 1 (dense-core/repeat-contact evidence dominates raw volume) and exchange 3 (convergence over distinct metrics, hence multiple comparable terms); valid for the small dense-core regime (dozens of nodes, hundreds of links), verified robust under +/-50% scaling of w_hard in this dataset; w_soft embedded in the camo term (0.25 of the final score), source: exchange 2 (cover-up talk = meta-communication clustered around suspicious topics, camouflage via innocuous topics); valid for topic structures where cover topics are identifiable from descriptions, as here; known-conspirator prior {18,21,7,43,54,67,49} and known-non {48,64,65,68,74,0,2,78}: source: task dataset (Requirement 1 statement); H={7,11,13}, S={1,4,6}: source: task dataset (Topics.csv descriptions).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The 7 known conspirators occupy ranks 1-6 and 11 (Alex 1, Elsie 2, Yao 3, Paul 4, Harvey 5, Ulf 6, Jean 11); the 8 known non-conspirators occupy ranks 13 (Darlene), 17 (Jia), 38 (Este), 40 (Paige), 53 (Tran), 60 (Ellin), 80 (Chris) and 83 (Gard, rank 83 out of 83 - tied at the bottom by score). Mean rank of known conspirators is 3.7 versus 44.9 for known non-conspirators, and the base list achieves clean separation (every known conspirator outranks every known non-conspirator). Top-15 unknown candidates, in priority order: Sherri (node 3, rank 7), Seeni (81, rank 8), Dwight (28, rank 10), William (50, rank 14), Shelley (35, rank 15), followed by Christina (47), Donald (41), Marion (13), Patricia (44), Neal (17). Managers: Delores (10) ranks 9, Jerome (16) ranks 7, Jerome (34) ranks 12, Gretchen (4) ranks 23, Gretchen (32) ranks 25 - Delores and both Jeromes sit above the median and inside the top 15, so all three senior managers show strong conspiracy indicators and should be investigated, with Delores (rank 9) the most prominent. Robustness (exchange 3 criterion): dropping topic 7, 11, or 13 one at a time leaves Alex, Elsie, Yao, Paul and one of Harvey/Ulf in the top five each time; scaling w_hard from 0.8 to 1.5 keeps the same seven unknowns in the top 10. The list is therefore stable under weight perturbation and topic removal. Limitations and biases: the 400 links are a censored sample, so absolute volumes understate true activity heterogeneously across people - all volume terms are rank-normalized to remove this; some known non-conspirators sit mid-list on residual traffic (Darlene rank 13, Jia 17: driven by camouflage traffic with core partners and a few hard-topic touches, not by hard-topic volume), which is exactly the false-accusation risk the supervisor warned about in the EZ case - these names should be treated as cleared-by-label, not as suspects; the model cannot use transcript content, so coded words (Spanish, discretion phrases) are only partially captured through topic 7's volume; betweenness on a sparse hard subgraph is sensitive to single-link removals for mid-list nodes, which is why it carries only 30% weight. The discriminating line (midpoint between the worst known conspirator's score, Jean 1.494, and the best known non-conspirator's, Darlene 1.362) separates the top ~15 from the rest, matching the EZ-case scale (conspiracy of roughly 5-8 of 10).

tasks.task_description: Requirement 2: How would the priority list change if new information shows that Topic 1 (company finances: stock price, earnings, liquid assets) is also connected to the conspiracy and that Chris is one of the conspirators?
tasks.task_analysis: Two changes to the requirement-1 pipeline: (1) topic 1 moves from the soft set {1,4,6} to the hard set, so H={1,7,11,13} and S={4,6} (the camouflage term is recomputed with the reduced soft set); (2) Chris (0) joins the known-conspirator prior, so P_i now also credits traffic with node 0, and the validation reference set gains Chris as a positive label. No other structural change; the method is deliberately modular so a new topic or a new label is a one-line rerun (python code/model.py --hard 1,7,11,13 --extra-known 0).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Identical to Requirement 1 with H={1,7,11,13}, S={4,6}, prior={18,21,7,43,54,67,49,0}, same weights (1.0, 0.3, 0.3, 0.25, 0.1). The change in H adds topic-1 volume into H_i and W_H, which re-ranks everyone with financial-topic traffic; adding Chris to the prior raises P_i for every node that messaged Chris (notably nodes 2, 21, 0's partners: 32, 40, 68, 2, 21) and lowers the relative discrimination of P_i for nodes with no Chris contact. Rerun outputs are in logs/model_req2.log.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Main changes versus Requirement 1: (a) Paul (43) and Yao (67) swap with Alex (21) at the very top - Paul becomes rank 1 because topic 1 traffic concentrates around the finance-focused core; (b) Gretchen (32) jumps from rank 25 to rank 5, the biggest mover, because her traffic combines hard topics 1, 7, 11, 13 with repeated contact with the prior set including Chris; (c) Neal (17) enters the top 15 (rank 11) on topic-1 volume and Chris contact; (d) Eric (22) rises to rank 13 on the recomputed camouflage term; (e) Dolores (10) falls slightly (rank 9 -> 10) as topic-1 volume spreads over more nodes and her camouflage component is unchanged; (f) Chris (0) himself now sits at rank 26 as a labeled conspirator with hard-topic volume - the model no longer needs to detect him, but his presence in the prior pulls his partners up. Clean separation of known conspirators from known non-conspirators weakens (best non-conspirator now outranks the worst conspirator, because Darlene, a non-conspirator, also carries topic-1 traffic and the reference set is tighter), while the mean known-conspirator rank (7.5) still beats the mean known-non rank (43.0) by a wide margin. Practical reading: the new information sharpens the finance thread of the conspiracy (topics 1 and 11 together describe the embezzlement/credit-card scheme), promotes the Gretchen node to a top-5 suspect, adds Neal and Eric to the surveillance shortlist, and slightly blurs the discriminating line - consistent with adding a genuinely conspiratorial topic that is also used by some innocent finance staff. The top-10 in the updated list: Paul, Yao, Alex, Ulf, Gretchen(32), Sherri, Harvey, Elsie, Jerome(16), Dwight.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 3: Explain how semantic network analysis and text analysis of the actual message content (if the original transcripts were obtainable) would improve the model and the categorization of the personnel, and whether any of these capabilities were used on the topic descriptions in Topics.csv to enhance the model.
tasks.task_analysis: Scope: qualitative methodology question, grounded in the concrete evidence available here (the 15 topic descriptions and the coded links). The explanation is organized around which limitations of the link-level model each technique attacks: (i) no access to words, (ii) topics are coarse bins, (iii) the camouflage pattern is only proxy-scored, (iv) no temporal or causal ordering, (v) no distinction between voluntary and coerced communication.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Semantic network analysis (SNA): build a concept graph from transcripts in which nodes are entities (people, systems, locations, amounts, dates, code words) and edges are co-occurrence or predicate relations ('remind X to be discreet about Y', 'make Z off-line longer'); then (1) entity-level alignment - link-level nodes (the 83 workers) become typed roles in the concept graph (organizer, planner, financier, lookout, cover); role assignment is a maximum-flow / bipartite matching between workers and roles, using each person's concept neighborhoods as evidence; (2) coded-language detection - Spanish code words and euphemisms form a dense concept cluster disconnected from any legitimate business ontology; members whose private messages route through that cluster are flagged directly, which replaces the current proxy camouflage term C_i with a direct measure; (3) relation mining - the conspiracy plan (topic 13: extend the off-line window for Paige/Ellin/Chris) is an explicit plan graph with actors and targets; target nodes (the three named non-conspirators) appear as objects, which confirms they are victims, not members, and raises the score of anyone issuing edges toward them as planners rather than as accidental traffic. Text analysis: (1) stylometric / authorship features (vocabulary richness, sentence length, punctuation) cluster messages by writer and detect single writers posting under multiple node identities - in this data, the duplicate names Jerome/Gretchen/Neal could not be disambiguated without transcripts; (2) sentiment and deception indicators - repeated reassurance scripts ('budget is fine', 'I will be fine', 'don't get him worried'), denial clusters, and meta-communication ('keep this quiet', 'not in front of Paige') are exactly the cover-up pattern identified in exchange 2; a classifier over these features yields a per-message suspicion prior that re-weights W_{s,e} by message instead of by topic, so a single covert message dominates a hundred routine ones; (3) temporal analysis - burst detection around the secret meeting (topic 7) and the planned off-line window (topic 13) identifies the operation's timeline and the coordination lag between organizer and executors, turning the static priority list into a time-ordered exposure ranking. Used on Topics.csv: yes, partially. The topic descriptions were read semantically to (a) confirm 7, 11, 13 as conspiratorial from their own text (secret meeting, system flaws, off-line plan) rather than by label alone, and (b) select the soft set {1,4,6} from description content (finances/liquid assets; the Paige argument; promotion politics) - this is precisely the SNA step of mapping coarse topic bins onto the covert-core concept cluster, done at the description level because transcripts are unavailable. What was NOT possible without transcripts: message-level re-weighting, coded-word detection, authorship disambiguation of the duplicate names, and plan-graph target identification.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Impact assessment: each upgrade targets a measured weakness of the link-level model. Direct coded-word detection would remove the largest single source of false positives (innocent people whose partners are in the core) by making the camouflage term evidence-based; plan-graph mining would resolve the Darlene/Jia/Gard/Ellin anomaly (high camouflage score, known innocent) by distinguishing traffic about targets from traffic within the ring; authorship analysis would settle whether the two Jeromes (16, 34) and two Grethchens (4, 32) are the same person or distinct, which materially changes the manager-conclusion (currently both Jerome nodes rank 7 and 12 and both Gretchen nodes rank 23/25 - if one pair is a single physical person, the effective manager suspicion concentrates further). For the DA, the strongest recommendation is a two-stage investigation protocol: the link-level priority list (this model) selects the top ~15 for surveillance and transcript collection; the semantic/text analysis then runs on the collected transcripts to convert surveillance candidates into prosecutable role assignments (who planned, who financed, who executed), which is the step that turns a ranked list into a case file and is also what makes the methodology scale to the supervisor's stated target of thousands of people and millions of words, where link-level metrics alone are too coarse.

tasks.task_description: Requirement 4: Write-up of the complete methodology for the DA's office (within the 20-page report constraint), including a discussion of how network, semantic and text analyses of message content help, and an explanation of the network modeling techniques used and why/how they generalize to identifying and prioritizing similar nodes in network databases of any type (e.g., infected cells in a biological network with heterogeneous image/chemical data and some pre-identified infected nodes).
tasks.task_analysis: Scope: consolidate the method, assumptions, validation, and generalization argument. The network-modeling techniques used are: (1) directed weighted aggregation of multi-topic edges, (2) subgraph extraction by topic class (hard/soft), (3) betweenness centrality as covert-channel brokerage, (4) ego-subgraph density as the dense-core signature, (5) label-adjacency (prior) scoring, (6) rank-normalized weighted-sum convergence with a separation-based decision line, (7) robustness protocol (weight sweep, topic leave-one-out, label leave-one-out). Generalization argument: every one of these is defined on any directed/undirected graph with edge attributes and a set of labeled positive/negative nodes; the crime-specific content enters only through the choice of which edge attributes count as 'hard' and which as 'soft', and through the domain prior that the anomaly is a small dense core. That is exactly the structure of the biological example posed in the requirement: nodes = cells, edges = signaling/co-localization links with heterogeneous image or chemical measurements as edge attributes, 'hard' attributes = measurements already flagged as infection indicators, pre-identified infected cells = the labeled positives, and the model outputs the same artifacts - a ranked priority list of candidate infected cells, a separating line, and a robustness report - with the dense-core assumption replaced (or validated) by the domain fact that infection spreads through local signaling neighborhoods.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: General template (the crime-busting model is the instance with H = suspicious topics): given G=(V,E,A) with edge attributes A, a labeled positive set P and negative set N, and attribute subsets A_hard, A_soft: (1) W_{s,e}^{hard} = sum over hard attributes of a_{s,e}; (2) five indicators H (hard volume), B (betweenness on W_hard), Pfrac (fraction of traffic with P), C (soft volume restricted to partners sharing hard traffic), K (ego density in W_hard); (3) rank-normalize each, combine S = sum_k w_k r_k with weights set by the evidence that each indicator contributes an independent signal (exchange 3: convergence); (4) decision line = midpoint of worst positive and best negative scores; (5) report = top-k list, separation statistic, and robustness under attribute leave-one-out and weight scaling. For the biological case: A_hard = infection-marker channels (e.g., a specific imaging contrast or cytokine reading), C becomes the 'camouflage' analogue (healthy-looking measurements on the same signaling partners as infected cells - i.e., cells that mimic healthy chemistry while sitting on infected signaling routes), and the duplicate-name issue becomes the cell-cluster identity issue, handled the same way (node identity, not image label).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Why the technique set transfers: it uses only graph structure and edge attributes, no crime-specific semantics, and its assumptions (small dense core, cover traffic, labeled seeds) are stated explicitly so they can be swapped per domain. Limitations that travel with it: (1) it ranks, it does not prove - the output is an investigation priority, and the separation statistic, not the absolute scores, is what must be checked per domain; (2) censored or sampled edges bias absolute volumes, handled by rank normalization, but a domain where sampling is strongly non-uniform (e.g., only the sickest cells are imaged) needs the prior terms re-weighted; (3) the dense-core prior fails for diffuse processes (chronic low-grade infection, or a conspiracy that spreads through many weak links) - the robustness protocol (leaving one hard attribute out at a time) is the early warning, since a diffuse process shows no stable top cluster under attribute leave-one-out; (4) in biology, the 'managers' analogue (hub cells whose role is coordination) are exactly the high-betweenness nodes, so the leader-nomination step maps directly: nominate the high-betweenness pre-identified-adjacent nodes as the coordinators of the infected region. For the DA report, the methodology contributes a reusable pipeline: label seeds -> attribute-classify edges -> five-converging-indicator score -> separation + robustness gate -> top-k action list, which is what the supervisor asked for as a world-best, scalable method for white-collar and other network-database investigations.
